# Large language models as a colleague {#llms}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* describe what a **large language model** (LLM) does and why its output
  varies and can be wrong;
* use an LLM through mirtverse to draft analysis code, write items and
  score responses, and see exactly what is sent to it;
* explain why every LLM output in testing needs a **check**, and use
  mirtverse's checks for wrong keys, weak distractors and machine-human
  agreement;
* make LLM work **reproducible** by recording and replaying responses, and
  say what to report about an LLM in a technical manual or paper.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[large language model](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#llm),
[prompt](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#prompt),
[hallucination](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#hallucination),
[human-in-the-loop](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#human-in-the-loop),
[automatic item generation](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#aig),
[automated scoring](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#automated-scoring).

```{r replay-on, include = FALSE}
# This chapter answers every language model request from the example
# recordings that come with mirtverse, so it builds offline and gives the
# same output every time. See mv_llm_replay().
old_llm <- suppressMessages(mv_llm_replay())
```

## The ideas

A large language model is a neural network trained on a very large amount
of text to predict the next piece of text. Given instructions and context,
the **prompt**, it continues them, and that one ability is enough to write
items, explain results, score essays against a rubric or draft code. Claude,
GPT and the open models that run on a laptop through Ollama all work this
way.

For a psychometrician, three properties matter more than how the network
works:

* **Its output is a sample.** The same prompt can give different answers on
  different runs and with different versions of the model. An LLM is not a
  function with a fixed value; it behaves more like a rater.
* **It can be fluently wrong.** A model can write an item with no correct
  option, invent a reference or misread a rubric, in the same confident
  style as a correct answer. Such errors are called **hallucinations**, and
  they are found only by checking.
* **What you send leaves your computer.** Unless the model runs locally,
  the prompt goes to a provider. Test content and response data may be
  confidential, so what is sent has to be a decision, not an accident.

These properties lead to the way mirtverse uses LLMs, which is also a good
rule for any testing program [@hao2024; @bulut2024]: The model drafts,
something else checks, and a person decides. Generated items are answered
again by a second, independent model call that does not see the key.
Machine scores must agree with human scores, overall and within groups,
before they count, following the framework of Williamson, Xi and Breyer
[-@williamson2012]. Anything the model is unsure about goes to a person.

mirtverse talks to models through the ellmer package. `mv_ask_setup()`
chooses a provider once: Claude or OpenAI with your own API key, or Ollama
for a free model that runs on your own computer. This chapter instead runs
in **replay mode**: `mv_llm_replay()` answers every request from a file of
recorded responses that comes with mirtverse, so the examples need no key,
no internet connection and give the same results for every reader. Those
responses were written by hand to show what a model returns, including a
few deliberate mistakes; they were not produced by a live model.

## Example 1: From a sentence to a tested script

`mv_ask()` turns a plain-language request into an analysis plan and the
plan into an R script built from tested templates. The model never writes
code and never sees the responses: It sees the request and a summary of the
columns. You can see that payload before anything is sent with
`dry_run = TRUE`:

```{r data-llms-1}
# mirt's Science data: 392 respondents, 4 attitude items scored 1 to 4.
resp <- Science
```

```{r}
request <- "Fit a graded response model to these attitude items, check the fit and explain the results."
mv_ask(request, data = resp, dry_run = TRUE)
```

The payload holds the request, the number of rows and, for each column, its
type, range, share missing and the role mirtverse guesses for it. With
`anonymize = TRUE` the column names are replaced by codes as well. Now the
real call, answered from the recording:

```{r}
s <- mv_ask(request, data = Science, ask = FALSE)
s$parser
s$plan$model
s$plan$assumptions
```

The model chose the graded response model, kept the default steps, and
stated two assumptions it made. Read them: An assumption is where a model
fills a gap in your request, and a wrong one gives a wrong analysis that
runs without error. The script itself is printed with `s`, and run with
`run_script(s)`.

## Example 2: Writing items, and catching the mistakes

The assessment pipeline writes items for the cells of a blueprint. Each
multiple-choice item comes with a key and a rationale for every option,
and is then checked by a second call that answers it blind.

```{r data-llms-2}
# A two-cell blueprint for a short Grade 7 numeracy quiz.
cells <- data.frame(content = c("Ratios and rates", "Measurement"),
                    cognitive = c("Apply", "Apply"), n = c(2, 2))
```

```{r}
p <- mv_pipeline("Grade 7 numeracy", verbose = FALSE)
p <- set_blueprint(p, cells, construct = "Grade 7 numeracy", use = "classroom diagnostic",
                   population = "Grade 7 students")
p <- suppressWarnings(generate_items(p, n = 2))
p$items[, c("id", "stem", "key", "verify_answer", "key_check")]
```

Two of the four items have problems. The writer keyed the garden item (G003)
as 84 m, which is the garden's area, but the question asks for the fence
around it, the perimeter of 38 m. The checking call answered B and the item
is flagged. In the millilitre item (G004), one distractor is a length, not
a volume, so no test taker would choose it:

```{r}
f <- flags(p, stage = "generation")
f[, c("check", "target", "level", "value")]
p$items$verify_note[3]
```

A `block` flag stops the pipeline at the next stage until a person fixes the
item or acknowledges the flag. The coverage flags are a reminder that items
are lost in review and field testing, so a pool needs more items than the
blueprint asks for. Notice what the checks do *not* do: They do not show
that the items measure Grade 7 numeracy, that they are fair, or that their
difficulty suits the test. Content review and a field test still do that.

## Example 3: Is a recording reproducible?

Replay makes a session reproducible in a strong sense: The same calls on
the same data give the same output, on any computer. It also makes the
limits of a recording visible. Change the request by one word and the
recording has no answer for it:

```{r}
tryCatch(
  suppressWarnings(generate_items(set_blueprint(mv_pipeline(verbose = FALSE), c(Algebra = 2)),
                                  n = 1)),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

For your own work, `mv_llm_record("session.json")` saves every request and
response while you use a live model, and `mv_llm_replay("session.json")`
plays them back. Keep the file with your analysis, as you would keep the
data and the code. When you report work that used an LLM, say which model
and version you used and when, give the prompts (mirtverse's are in its
source code and in the recording), say what was sent and what was not, and
describe how the outputs were checked.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Run `mv_ask(request, data = Science, dry_run = TRUE, anonymize = TRUE)`.
   What is still sent? Is anything in it confidential for your own data?
2. List the recordings that come with mirtverse with `mv_llm_recordings()`.
   Which mirtverse functions made them?
3. In Example 2, fix the miskeyed item with `p$items$key[3] <- "B"` and
   acknowledge the flag with `acknowledge()`. Why does mirtverse ask for a
   person to acknowledge a flag rather than clear it automatically?
4. Your program wants an LLM to score 20,000 short answers next spring. Name
   three pieces of evidence you would ask for before the machine scores
   count, and one group of test takers you would check separately.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
mv_ask(request, data = Science, dry_run = TRUE, anonymize = TRUE)
mv_llm_recordings()[, c("function_name", "prompt_start")]
```

1. The request (with column names coded), the number of rows and the
   summary of each column (type, distinct values, range, share missing,
   guessed role) are still sent. Category labels are left out. Individual
   responses are never sent. For a confidential test, the request itself or
   the column names may give away content, which is why `anonymize = TRUE`
   exists; a local model through Ollama sends nothing at all.
2. `mv_ask()`, `generate_items()` (twice, one call per blueprint cell),
   `verify_items()` (once per item, called by `generate_items()`) and
   `score_open()` (once per batch of 10 responses, from the example in
   `system.file("replay", "examples.R", package = "mirtverse")`).
3. A check can only say that something looks wrong; deciding whether it is,
   and what to do, is a professional judgement. Recording who acknowledged
   which flag, and why, is part of the evidence for the test.
4. For example: Agreement between machine and human scores on a sample of
   double-scored responses, compared with agreement between two humans
   [@williamson2012]; the standardized mean difference between machine and
   human scores; and the same statistics within groups, such as English
   language learners, whose answers may be shorter or phrased differently
   at the same level of understanding. `score_open()` reports all of these.

</details>

```{r replay-off, include = FALSE}
options(old_llm)
```

## Further reading {-}

Hao et al. [-@hao2024] describe what large language models change in
testing, from item development to score reporting. Bulut et al.
[-@bulut2024] discuss the opportunities and the ethical questions, and
Williamson, Xi and Breyer [-@williamson2012] remain the reference for
evaluating automated scores.
